article.headline: Guatemalan tiger rump tarantula care guide
article.description: A detailed guide to keeping Davus pentaloris: size, terrarium, substrate, temperature, humidity, feeding, hairs and moulting.

name: Guatemalan tiger rump tarantula
lead: A small, lively tarantula from Central America with orange stripes on its abdomen. Easy to care for and a great choice for a first spider.
photoAlt: Guatemalan tiger rump tarantula (Davus pentaloris) - NS Reptiles Novi Sad
intro: The Guatemalan tiger rump tarantula (Davus pentaloris) comes from southern Mexico and Guatemala. It is named after the orange stripes across its dark abdomen. It is small, grows quickly and eats readily, which makes it interesting to watch and rewarding for beginners - but it is fast and skittish, so it is better observed than handled. To get started, we also offer a tarantula starter kit with an enclosure and substrate.

boxes.title: Origin and habitat
p: It comes from Central America - southern Mexico and Guatemala - where it lives on the forest floor, in burrows under roots, stones and leaf litter.

boxes.title: Size and appearance
p: A small to medium tarantula: adult females reach a leg span of about 10–12 cm, while males are slimmer and slightly smaller. The body and legs are dark, almost black, and the abdomen carries the orange stripes that give it its name.

boxes.title: Behaviour
p: Mostly calm, but fast and skittish - when startled it usually bolts into its hide. It likes to dig and is often seen at the entrance to its burrow. It is more active than many other tarantulas, so it is on display more often.

boxes.title: Terrarium
p: This is a terrestrial species, so it needs a horizontal terrarium - floor space matters more than height. An enclosure with a floor of about 30×20 cm is enough for an adult. Leave only a few centimetres more than the spider's leg span above the substrate: a fall can rupture the abdomen and be fatal. The lid must close tightly, and ventilation should be both on the sides and on top. Spiderlings are kept in smaller containers, in proportion to their size.

boxes.title: Substrate
p: Provide 8–10 cm of substrate for digging: coco peat or a mix of peat and fertiliser-free soil. The lower layer should be slightly moist, while part of the surface can stay drier.

boxes.title: Hide and decor
p: A half cork bark or a piece of bark as a hide, a shallow water dish and a few dry leaves or artificial plants are enough. Place heavier items on the bottom before adding substrate, so they cannot fall on the spider while it digs. Do not overcrowd the enclosure.

boxes.title: Temperature and light
p: Room temperature of about 22–27 °C suits it. If it gets colder in winter, put a heat mat on a side or back wall, never under the substrate - the spider escapes heat by digging down, so heating from below could overheat it. No special lighting or UVB is needed; avoid direct sunlight.

boxes.title: Humidity and water
p: Humidity of about 65–75% suits it. Water one corner of the substrate from time to time instead of spraying the spider. A shallow dish of clean water should always be in the enclosure.

boxes.title: Prey
p: It feeds on live insects: crickets, roaches (e.g. dubia), locusts and similar prey. Prey should not be larger than the spider's abdomen. Do not feed wild-caught insects, as they may carry parasites and pesticides.

boxes.title: Feeding frequency
p: Adults need food once a week or less, spiderlings twice a week with smaller prey. Remove prey that is not eaten within a day. It is normal for a tarantula to refuse food for weeks before a moult - do not offer food then.

boxes.title: Urticating hairs
p: Like other tarantulas from the Americas, it has urticating hairs on the abdomen that it flicks off with its legs when threatened. On the skin they cause itching and redness, and in the eyes serious irritation. Keep your face away when working in the enclosure and wash your hands afterwards. This species flicks hairs moderately - it would rather run than defend itself.

boxes.title: Venom
p: The venom of this species is not dangerous to a healthy person - a bite is comparable to a bee or wasp sting: pain, redness and swelling that pass. As with a bee sting, an allergic reaction is possible; if breathing becomes difficult or swelling spreads, seek medical help immediately.

boxes.title: Handling
p: We do not recommend handling. A fall from just a few dozen centimetres can be fatal for a tarantula, and a frightened spider may bite or flick hairs. To move it, guide the spider into a clear container and cover it with a piece of card. Keep the enclosure out of reach of children and pets.

boxes.title: Growth and lifespan
p: It grows moderately fast and reaches adult size relatively early for a tarantula. Females live about 10–15 years, males much less - usually a year or two after maturing.

boxes.title: Moulting
p: A tarantula grows by moulting. Before a moult it stops eating and its abdomen darkens. It usually moults lying on its back - this is normal and not a sign of death, so do not touch it. After the moult wait at least a week before feeding, until the new exoskeleton and fangs harden. No live prey may be left in the enclosure at that time.

boxes.title: Possible problems
p: The biggest risks are falls, dehydration and live prey left in during a moult. A spider pulling its legs under its body is a serious sign - check that it has water and contact an experienced breeder or an exotic animal vet. Mould and mites appear in an overly wet, poorly ventilated enclosure with food leftovers.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about the guatemalan tiger rump tarantula

items.q: Is the guatemalan tiger rump tarantula venomous?
items.a: It is not dangerous to a healthy person - a bite is similar to a bee sting. The bigger nuisance is the urticating hairs from the abdomen, which irritate the skin and eyes.

items.q: How big does the guatemalan tiger rump tarantula get?
items.a: Adult females reach a leg span of about 10–12 cm; males are slightly smaller.

items.q: How long does the guatemalan tiger rump tarantula live?
items.a: Females about 10–15 years, males much less.

items.q: What does the guatemalan tiger rump tarantula eat?
items.a: Live insects of the right size - crickets, roaches and locusts. Adults only need feeding once a week or less.

items.q: Is the guatemalan tiger rump tarantula good for beginners?
items.a: Yes - it is easy to care for, eats readily and is undemanding. Just keep in mind that it is fast and skittish, so it is for watching, not handling.

items.q: Can you handle a guatemalan tiger rump tarantula?
items.a: We do not recommend it. A fall can be fatal for the spider, and a frightened tarantula may bite or flick irritating hairs. Use a container to move it.
